newsitem.title: POLAND: Flood alert eases in Central Europe.
newsitem.headline: Flood alert eases in Central Europe.

text.p: Flood-hit residents of central Europe, exhausted from two weeks of floods that killed around 100 people, took hope on Monday from weather forecasts suggesting that the worst might soon be over.
But downstream on the river Oder dividing Germany and Poland some communities still faced grim battles with encroaching water and possible evacuation.

"Despite rains on Sunday and on Monday, the situation is much better than it was and everything suggests it will improve," the spokesman of Poland's flood crisis committee, Krzysztof Pomes, told Reuters. "Water levels are tending to subside on most rivers," he said.
Rain drenching the flood-stricken region of Silesia on Monday will gradually subside until Wednesday and the rest of the week is likely to be sunny, forecasters said.

Some areas in southwest and south Poland remained under the water that inundated more than 1,000 towns and villages. The death toll was at least 50 people and 140,000 have been forced to evacuate their homes.

On the German side of the Oder, which is flowing up to three metres (nine feet) above its usual level in some places, workers fought overnight to repair dykes to prevent the river breaking its banks and flooding thousands of hectares.
Matthias Platzeck, environment minister in the eastern German state of Brandenburg, said plans were being made for possible evacuation of the region if dykes along the Oder's banks failed to hold.
About 20,000 people live in Germany's Oderbruch area on the Polish border -- a low-lying area that would face certain flooding if the river broke its banks.

Brandenburg interior minister Alwin Ziel said he expected the floods, to result in high water levels in the east German region for the next two weeks at least and there were doubts over whether the dykes would hold.
The flood wave on the Oder, known in Poland as the Odra, was due to hit the the northwestern Polish port of Szczecin, but was unlikely to swamp the city, flood control officials said.
Poland's biggest river, the Wisla, was calm. Smaller mountain rivers overflowed in Nowy Sacz and Jelenia Gora provinces, where floods may still hit several towns and villages.
"People are working themselves into a sweat. Many of them lost all their possessions," Grzegorz Ossowski, a local radio reporter in the southwestern city of Walbrzych, told Reuters.
New health dangers faced the some southwestern Polish cities such as Wroclaw, where a lack of clean water prompted fears of an epidemic of dysentery.
Most major rivers in the east of the Czech Republic, where 46 people have died in the past two weeks, were falling on Monday.

"We expect the water levels to continue to fall," meteorologist Frantisek Sopko told Reuters. He said the light rain on Monday morning was likely to give way to showers later and on Tuesday with little or no rain forecast for Wednesday and Thursday.
However, several thousand residents of the town of Otrokovice were warned to prepare for evacuation as the Morava river rose.

As the floodwaters recede, Czechs are faced with a massive clean-up operation. The floods have destroyed some 1,600 houses and damaged 10,000 in 500 towns and villages, Deputy Prime Minister Josef Lux said at the weekend.

The floods also cut road, rail and telecommunicatioons links. Czech Television said the main eastward railway line to the city of Ostrava was restored on Monday, two weeks after an accident which injured at least 64 passengers.
Further south along central Europe's main waterway the Danube, water levels continued to rise on Monday but were not expected to reach dangerous levels, the authorities said.

Hungary's Flood Control Centre told the Hungarian news agency MTI the river had risen 60 cm (two feet) overnight and a full flood alert had been issued at the wetlands of Szigetkoz, which straddle the border with Slovakia.
Lower-level alerts were issued further downriver as far as Budapest while ferry services between the city of Esztergom and the Slovak town of Sturovo were to be suspended on Tuesday.
The centre said earlier the Danube was expected to rise by a daily 70 cm (just over two feet) on Monday and Tuesday in Budapest and would peak at 710 cm (23 feet) on Wednesday.
Such levels involve the closing of sections of Budapest's waterside highways from Monday but pose no threat of flooding to the capital.
The stretch of Danube river in Austria from the German border town of Passau through to Linz was reopened to shipping early on Monday morning, Austrian river police said.
However, roughly 50 km (30 miles) of the Danube between the Slovak border and the Freudenau lock east of Vienna remained closed.
The stretch is expected to be reopened by the end of Monday.
